parts.title: Talk to a model
parts.description: Run a model, call it from code, compare models with numbers, and give one tools.

parts.title: Give it knowledge
parts.description: Search by meaning, answer from your own documents, measure it, and fine-tune a small model.

parts.title: Build the harness
parts.description: The parts around the model: permissions, budgets, tool servers, and checks on generated code.

parts.title: Make it reliable
parts.description: Grading, traces, memory, flows that survive a restart, parallel work, and safe self-improvement.

parts.title: Deliver to a customer
parts.description: Choose the right problem, attack your own work, control every tool call, ship it, and hand it over.

parts.title: Foundations
parts.description: Get oriented, confirm your CLI, and make a project that Flisk can understand.

parts.title: Project structure
parts.description: Learn how projects, stacks, and resources fit together.

parts.title: First service
parts.description: Create a backend resource and inspect the generated contract.

01-installed.title: Is Flisk installed?
01-installed.goal: Check that the Flisk CLI is on your PATH and that your machine can run a local stack.
01-installed.build: A machine that passes flisk doctor, ready for the next lab.
needs: Docker Desktop, Colima or OrbStack (only for container stacks)

steps.task: Install the CLI and print its version
steps.explain: Install it once with npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk. Every later lab assumes this command works.
steps.expect: A version number such as 1.4.61 prints.

steps.task: Check your machine
steps.explain: Doctor checks Docker, Tilt, free ports and your project. It does not check any cloud cluster.
steps.expect: Each check shows a green tick. A red line names what is missing and the command that fixes it; run that and try again.

02-scaffold.title: Scaffold a project
02-scaffold.goal: Create a new Flisk project in an empty folder.
02-scaffold.build: A project folder that Flisk recognises, ready for its first service.

steps.task: Make an empty folder and go into it
steps.expect: Your prompt now ends in my-app.

steps.task: Create the project
steps.explain: --yes accepts the defaults, so nothing asks you questions.
steps.expect: Flisk says the project was created, and ls shows package.json, AGENTS.md and a services folder.

03-backend.title: Add a backend resource
03-backend.goal: Add your first backend service to the project and see Flisk pick it up.
03-backend.build: An api service in services/pre-alpha/api, counted in flisk status.

steps.task: Add a backend called api
steps.explain: A resource is one service. Flisk writes its service.json for you, so you never hand-write container files.
steps.cmd: flisk resource api --type backend --stack pre-alpha --path services/pre-alpha/api --yes
steps.expect: Flisk says the api resource was created, and services/pre-alpha/api holds a service.json.

steps.task: Check that Flisk sees it
steps.expect: Stacks shows pre-alpha: 1 resource. Services stay stopped until you run flisk up pre-alpha.

10-local-model.title: Run a model on your laptop
10-local-model.goal: Run a small open model on your own machine and call it two ways: from the terminal and over HTTP.
10-local-model.build: A local model that answers on http://localhost:11434, with no account and no bill.

steps.task: Install Ollama and pull a small model
steps.explain: Everything in this course can start on a model this size. Bigger models come later, when you can measure whether they are worth it.
steps.expect: The list shows llama3.2 with a size of about 2 GB.

steps.task: Ask it one question from the terminal
steps.cmd: ollama run llama3.2 "In one sentence, what is a token?"
steps.expect: One sentence prints and you get your prompt back.

steps.task: Call the same model over HTTP
steps.explain: This is the same request shape most hosted models accept. Every later lab is this call with more around it.
steps.cmd: curl -s http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"llama3.2","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hi in three words."}]}'
steps.expect: JSON comes back with the answer under choices[0].message.content and a usage block that counts prompt and completion tokens.

11-chat-api.title: Call a hosted model and read the bill
11-chat-api.goal: Send a chat request to a hosted model from your own script, keep a conversation going, and print what each call costs.
11-chat-api.build: chat.py: a 60-line chat client that prints the answer, the token counts and the cost of every call.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Put your key and a model name in the environment
steps.explain: Keep the key in your shell or a .env file that git ignores. Never paste it into a script.
steps.expect: It prints ready. MODEL holds a model id you picked from the OpenRouter model list (filter by price: free).

steps.task: Write chat.py: one system message, one user message, print the answer and the usage
steps.explain: Use the openai package with base_url set to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1. The same script talks to Ollama if you point base_url at http://localhost:11434/v1.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai chat.py "Explain a context window to a ten year old"
steps.expect: An answer prints, then one line with prompt tokens and completion tokens.

steps.task: Add a --chat mode that resends the whole conversation each turn
steps.explain: The model remembers nothing. The conversation is a list you keep and send again, which is why long chats cost more per turn.
steps.expect: Tell it your name in turn one and ask for it in turn two: it answers correctly, and the prompt token count grows every turn.

steps.task: Print the cost of each call from the model's listed prices
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai chat.py "Give me three names for a parcel company"
steps.expect: A cost line prints in dollars. On a free model it is 0, so also print what the same call would cost on one paid model you name.

12-compare-models.title: Pick a model with numbers
12-compare-models.goal: Run the same five tasks on three models and choose one from a table of speed, cost and quality.
12-compare-models.build: bench.py and results.csv: 15 rows you scored yourself, and a three-line DECISION.md.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Write five real tasks from your own work, one per line
steps.explain: Public leaderboards rank models on other people's tasks. Five of your own tell you more than any of them.
steps.expect: Five lines. Each is something you would really ask, with an answer you can judge.

steps.task: Write bench.py: every prompt on one local and two hosted models, timed
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai bench.py && column -s, -t results.csv | head -20
steps.expect: 15 rows, each with model, prompt number, seconds, tokens in, tokens out and cost.

steps.task: Score every answer from 1 to 5 without looking at the model name
steps.explain: Hide the model column while you score. Knowing which model wrote an answer changes how you grade it.
steps.expect: One line per model: average score, average seconds, total cost.

steps.task: Write down your pick and the number that decided it
steps.expect: Three lines: the model, the reason as a number from your table, and what would make you switch.

13-tool-loop.title: Give a model tools: the loop from scratch
13-tool-loop.goal: Write the loop that lets a model call your functions, with no framework, so you know what every framework is doing for you.
13-tool-loop.build: agent.py: about 80 lines that answer questions about a folder by listing and reading files.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough), or Ollama with a model that supports tools

steps.task: Describe two tools to the model: list_dir and read_file
steps.explain: A tool is a name, a sentence and a JSON schema. The model never runs anything: it only asks.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai agent.py --once "Which files are in this folder?"
steps.expect: The script prints a tool call the model asked for (list_dir with a path) and stops. Nothing is executed yet.

steps.task: Run the tool the model asked for and send the result back
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai agent.py --once "Which files are in this folder?"
steps.expect: Now the answer lists the real files in the folder.

steps.task: Loop until the model stops asking for tools, with a limit of 8 turns
steps.explain: The turn limit is your first safety control. Without it a confused model loops until your budget is gone.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai agent.py "Which file in this folder has the most lines, and how many?"
steps.expect: It lists the folder, reads several files, then names the right file. Check the number with wc -l.

steps.task: Print one line per step: who spoke, which tool, how many tokens
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai agent.py --trace "How many Python files are here?"
steps.expect: A numbered trace prints before the answer, and reading a file that does not exist shows up as a tool error the model recovers from, not a crash.

14-structured-output.title: Get data back, not prose
14-structured-output.goal: Turn messy customer emails into validated records your code can trust.
14-structured-output.build: extract.py: reads an email, returns a checked Claim record, and retries once when the model gets the shape wrong.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Write ten short customer emails about parcels: lost, damaged, late
steps.explain: This is Parcel Desk, the small courier the rest of the course works for. Its customers email in claims for refunds.
steps.expect: Ten files. Make two of them awkward: one with no parcel number, one with two amounts.

steps.task: Define a Claim: parcel id, reason (lost, damaged or late), amount, currency
steps.cmd: uv run --with pydantic python -c "from extract import Claim; print(Claim.model_json_schema()['required'])"
steps.expect: The required fields print. Reason only accepts the three values.

steps.task: Ask the model for JSON in that shape and validate it
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with pydantic extract.py samples/
steps.expect: Ten lines of valid JSON, one per email. The email with no parcel number has a null id, not an invented one.

steps.task: On a validation error, send the error back to the model once, then give up loudly
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with pydantic extract.py samples/; echo "exit $?"
steps.expect: Exit 0 when all ten validate. Break one on purpose (ask for a fourth reason value) and the exit code is not 0.

20-embeddings.title: Search by meaning
20-embeddings.goal: Turn text into vectors and find the closest sentences, first in memory and then in a database.
20-embeddings.build: search.py: finds the right sentence even when it shares no words with the question.

steps.task: Pull an embedding model and embed one sentence
steps.cmd: ollama pull nomic-embed-text && curl -s http://localhost:11434/api/embed -d '{"model":"nomic-embed-text","input":"my box arrived crushed"}' | head -c 200
steps.expect: JSON with an embeddings array of numbers.

steps.task: Write 30 sentences about parcels and rank them against a question by cosine similarity
steps.cmd: uv run --with numpy --with requests search.py "my box arrived crushed"
steps.expect: The top three are about damage, though none of them contains the word crushed.

steps.task: Start Postgres with pgvector
steps.cmd: docker run -d --name learn-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=learn -p 5433:5432 pgvector/pgvector:pg17 && sleep 5 && docker exec learn-pg psql -U postgres -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector; SELECT extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname='vector';"
steps.expect: One row with the extension version.

steps.task: Store the vectors in a table and run the same search in SQL
steps.cmd: uv run --with numpy --with requests --with "psycopg[binary]" search.py --db "my box arrived crushed"
steps.expect: The same top three as the in-memory search.

21-rag.title: Answer from your documents, with sources
21-rag.goal: Build a question answerer that reads your own documents, names the file each answer came from, and says so when the answer is not there.
21-rag.build: ingest.py and ask.py over six pages of Parcel Desk policy.

steps.task: Write six short policy pages: refunds, damage, lost parcels, international, time limits, exclusions
steps.expect: Six files, each under 300 words, with at least one concrete number (days, amounts).

steps.task: Split each page into chunks and store them with their file name
steps.expect: It prints how many chunks it stored per file. Running it twice does not double the rows.

steps.task: Fetch the four closest chunks and answer only from them, naming the files
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with requests --with "psycopg[binary]" ask.py "How many days do I have to report a damaged parcel?"
steps.expect: The number from your damage page, followed by the file name it came from.

steps.task: Ask something the pages do not cover
steps.explain: An answerer that guesses is worse than no answerer. This refusal is the most important line in your prompt.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with requests --with "psycopg[binary]" ask.py "Do you ship live animals to Mars?"
steps.expect: It says the documents do not cover this. It does not make up a policy.

22-rag-evals.title: Measure retrieval before you tune it
22-rag-evals.goal: Put a number on how often the right page is found, then change one thing and see if the number moves.
22-rag-evals.build: evalset.jsonl with 20 questions, eval.py, and a before and after table.

steps.task: Write 20 questions, each with the file that holds the answer
steps.expect: 20 lines. Include five that use different words from the page.

steps.task: Print recall at 4 and the mean reciprocal rank
steps.explain: Recall at 4: how often the right page is in the four chunks you fetch. Reciprocal rank: 1 if it is first, 1/2 if second, and so on.
steps.expect: Two numbers between 0 and 1, and a list of the questions that missed.

steps.task: Change one thing: chunk size, overlap, or a rerank step
steps.cmd: uv run --with requests --with "psycopg[binary]" eval.py evalset.jsonl --label after
steps.expect: The same two numbers for the new setup.

steps.task: Write the before and after in a table and keep or revert the change
steps.expect: Two rows and a one-line decision. A change that does not move the number is reverted.

23-dataset-baseline.title: Build a dataset and a baseline to beat
23-dataset-baseline.goal: Make a small labelled dataset and score two cheap baselines on it, so later work has a number to beat.
23-dataset-baseline.build: data/ with train, validation and test files, and two accuracy numbers on the same test rows.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Collect 300 claim emails labelled lost, damaged or late
steps.explain: Reading your own data is the step people skip and the one that pays most. Note how many of your 30 were wrong.
steps.expect: 300 lines of text and label. Have a model write them if you have none, then read 30 yourself and fix wrong labels.

steps.task: Shuffle once with a fixed seed and split 240, 30, 30
steps.expect: 240, 30 and 30 lines. No email appears in two files.

steps.task: Train word counts plus logistic regression and score it on the test rows
steps.expect: An accuracy number and a 3 by 3 table of which label was mistaken for which.

steps.task: Score a hosted model on the same 30 rows with no training
steps.expect: A second accuracy number and its cost. Write both in RESULTS.md: this is the bar.

24-fine-tune.title: Fine-tune a small open model
24-fine-tune.goal: Train a small adapter (LoRA) on your dataset and prove with the test rows whether it beat the baselines.
24-fine-tune.build: A trained adapter and a three-row table: classic baseline, untuned model, tuned model.
needs: An Apple Silicon Mac (mlx-lm) or a free cloud notebook with a GPU (PEFT)

steps.task: Convert train and validation rows to chat format: the email in, the label out
steps.expect: One JSON line with a messages list: a user message and a one-word assistant message.

steps.task: Score the untuned small model on the test rows
steps.expect: An accuracy number, usually below your classic baseline.

steps.task: Train an adapter and log training and validation loss every 50 steps
steps.explain: An adapter trains a few million numbers and leaves the model untouched, which is why it fits on a laptop.
steps.expect: Both losses went down from the first line of the log. The adapter is a small file, not a new model.

steps.task: Find the step where validation loss stops falling and keep that checkpoint
steps.explain: When training loss keeps falling and validation loss turns up, the model is memorising. Stop there.
steps.expect: A tuned accuracy on the same 30 rows. In RESULTS.md, say which step you kept and why.

30-harness.title: A model plus a harness
30-harness.goal: Wrap your tool loop in the parts that make it usable: instructions in a file, a permission question, a budget and a log.
30-harness.build: harness.py: your loop from lab 13 that asks before it writes, stops at a budget, and logs every message.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Move the instructions into SYSTEM.md and load them at start
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai harness.py "What are your rules?"
steps.expect: It answers from SYSTEM.md. Change a rule in the file and the answer changes with no code edit.

steps.task: Add a write_file tool that asks y or n before it runs
steps.explain: Reading is safe to allow. Writing, running commands and spending money ask first. That one split is most of agent safety.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai harness.py "Create notes.txt with one line saying hello"
steps.expect: It asks before writing. Answer n: no file appears and the model is told it was refused.

steps.task: Stop the run at a turn limit and a token limit
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai harness.py --max-tokens 2000 "Read every file here and summarise each one"
steps.expect: It stops with a clear message that the budget ran out, and says how far it got.

steps.task: Append every message and tool result to a log file
steps.expect: One JSON line per message, with a timestamp and token counts. You can replay a run from the file alone.

31-coding-agent-rules.title: Put a coding agent on rails
31-coding-agent-rules.goal: Write the instruction file a coding agent reads, and use permission modes so it plans before it edits.
31-coding-agent-rules.build: An AGENTS.md under 60 lines in a repo of yours, and one small change made by a coding agent under your rules.
needs: A coding agent you already use (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or similar)
A small git repo with a test command

steps.task: Write AGENTS.md: what the repo is, the test and lint commands, three rules, known traps
steps.explain: Write what a new colleague gets wrong in week one. Leave out what the code already says.
steps.expect: Under 60 lines. Every command in it runs as written.

steps.task: Give the agent a small issue in its read-only or plan mode
steps.expect: Nothing changed on disk, and you have a plan that names the files it will touch.

steps.task: Allow edits and let it carry out the plan
steps.expect: The diff touches only the files the plan named, and the agent ran your test command without being told to in the prompt.

steps.task: Add the first thing it got wrong to AGENTS.md
steps.expect: A second commit to AGENTS.md. The file grows from real mistakes, not guesses.

32-mcp-server.title: Build a tool server any assistant can use
32-mcp-server.goal: Publish your tools over the Model Context Protocol so any assistant that speaks it can call them.
32-mcp-server.build: server.py: an MCP server with two Parcel Desk tools, tested in the inspector and connected to a coding agent.

steps.task: Write a server with two tools: lookup_parcel and list_claims
steps.explain: The server runs as a child process and talks over standard input and output. Nothing listens on the network yet.
steps.expect: The inspector opens and lists both tools with a description and typed arguments.

steps.task: Call lookup_parcel with an id that does not exist
steps.expect: The tool returns a plain sentence saying the parcel was not found. No stack trace reaches the caller.

steps.task: Add the server to your coding agent and ask about a parcel
steps.cmd: claude mcp add parcel -- uv run --with mcp server.py && claude mcp list
steps.expect: The server is listed as connected, and the agent answers a parcel question by calling your tool. Other agents have their own add command.

steps.task: Serve the same tools over HTTP so a remote assistant can reach them
steps.explain: Local process for tools on your machine, HTTP for tools shared by a team. Flisk scaffolds the second kind with flisk resource <name> --type mcp.
steps.expect: With the server started in HTTP mode, the inspector connects by URL and shows the same two tools.

33-hardening.title: Make AI-written code safe to merge
33-hardening.goal: Set up the checks that catch a coding agent's mistakes before a person has to: lint, types, tests with a coverage floor, and a commit hook.
33-hardening.build: A repo where a bad commit is refused on your machine, by tools rather than by review.
needs: Any small Python project (the harness from lab 30 works)

steps.task: Add a linter and a type checker and fix what they find
steps.cmd: uv run ruff check . && uv run pyright
steps.expect: Both exit 0.

steps.task: Write tests until coverage reaches 80 percent, and make less than that a failure
steps.expect: Tests pass and the coverage line shows 80 percent or more.

steps.task: Run all three before every commit
steps.expect: The hook runs lint, types and tests and passes.

steps.task: Try to commit a file with an unused import
steps.explain: Checks a machine runs are the only review that scales with the amount of code an agent writes.
steps.expect: The commit is refused and the exit code is not 0. Add the three commands to AGENTS.md so the agent runs them itself.

34-open-weights.title: Choose and run open models
34-open-weights.goal: Measure what a smaller, more compressed copy of a model costs you in quality and gives you in speed and memory.
34-open-weights.build: A table for one model at two compression levels: size, memory, tokens per second, and your score.

steps.task: Pull the same model at 4-bit and 8-bit
steps.explain: Quantising stores each weight in fewer bits. The file shrinks and runs faster; some accuracy is lost. How much is what you measure.
steps.cmd: ollama pull llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M && ollama pull llama3.2:3b-instruct-q8_0 && ollama list
steps.expect: Two entries for the same model. The 8-bit one is clearly larger on disk.

steps.task: Time both on one prompt
steps.cmd: ollama run llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M --verbose "Write a haiku about parcels"
steps.expect: After the answer, a block of timings with an eval rate in tokens per second. Run it for both and note the two rates.

steps.task: See what is loaded and how much memory it takes
steps.expect: The loaded model with its size in memory and whether it runs on the GPU.

steps.task: Run your five prompts from lab 12 on both and score them blind
steps.expect: A table with size, memory, speed and average score for each, and the one you would ship.

40-evals-judge.title: Grade with a judge you have checked
40-evals-judge.goal: Use a model to grade answers, and prove first that it grades the way you do.
40-evals-judge.build: labels.csv with 40 decisions you graded by hand, judge.py, and an agreement score.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Grade 40 claim decisions yourself: right or wrong
steps.expect: 41 lines: a header and 40 rows of claim, decision and your grade. Make about a quarter of them wrong decisions.

steps.task: Write a judge prompt and grade the same 40 with a model
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with scikit-learn judge.py labels.csv
steps.expect: A 2 by 2 table of your grade against the judge's, with precision and recall.

steps.task: Print agreement beyond chance (Cohen's kappa)
steps.explain: Plain agreement flatters a judge when most answers are right. Kappa takes out the agreement you would get by luck.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with scikit-learn judge.py labels.csv --kappa
steps.expect: A number up to 1. Below 0.6, read the rows you disagree on, tighten the judge prompt and run again.

steps.task: Decide which mistake is worse: paying a bad claim or refusing a good one
steps.expect: A price on each mistake, and the judge setting you chose because of it.

41-tracing.title: See every step: traces
41-tracing.goal: Record every model call and tool call of a run so you can see where the time and money went.
41-tracing.build: A local tracing dashboard showing one run of your harness, step by step, with cost.

steps.task: Start Langfuse on your machine
steps.cmd: git clone https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse.git && cd langfuse && docker compose up -d
steps.expect: The containers start. The first start pulls several images and takes a few minutes.

steps.task: Check that it answers
steps.expect: 200. Open http://localhost:3000, create a local account and a project, and copy its two keys into your environment.

steps.task: Send one span per model call and per tool call from your harness
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with langfuse harness.py "Which file here is the largest?"
steps.expect: One new trace in the dashboard, with tool calls nested under the run and token counts on each model call.

steps.task: Find the slowest step and the most expensive step of that run
steps.expect: Two lines naming each step, with its seconds and cost, and one idea to cut each.

42-memory.title: Memory that outlives the conversation
42-memory.goal: Let your assistant store facts and find them in a later session, without one customer seeing another's.
42-memory.build: Two tools, remember and recall, backed by a local vector database with one space per customer.

steps.task: Start Qdrant
steps.cmd: docker run -d --name learn-qdrant -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant && sleep 3 && curl -s http://localhost:6333/collections
steps.expect: JSON with "status":"ok" and an empty list of collections.

steps.task: Add remember(fact) and recall(question) to your harness
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with qdrant-client --with requests harness.py --customer ana "Remember that I prefer deliveries after 6pm"
steps.expect: It confirms the fact was stored, and the collections list now has one entry.

steps.task: Start a new session and ask about it
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with qdrant-client --with requests harness.py --customer ana "When should you deliver to me?"
steps.expect: A fresh process answers after 6pm.

steps.task: Ask the same question as another customer
steps.explain: Filter by customer in the database query, not in the prompt. A prompt can be talked out of a rule; a filter cannot.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with qdrant-client --with requests harness.py --customer ben "When should you deliver to me?"
steps.expect: It does not know. Ana's fact never appears in Ben's session.

43-durable.title: Survive a restart, wait for a person
43-durable.goal: Build a claim flow that saves its place after every step, pauses for a human on large amounts, and pays exactly once.
43-durable.build: claim_flow.py: intake, decide, approve, pay, with its state in Postgres.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Write the four steps as a graph and run one small claim end to end
steps.cmd: uv run --with langgraph --with langgraph-checkpoint-postgres --with "psycopg[binary]" --with openai claim_flow.py start --thread t0 --amount 20
steps.expect: The claim is paid in one run, and a payments table has one row for t0.

steps.task: Stop and wait for approval when the amount is over 100
steps.cmd: uv run --with langgraph --with langgraph-checkpoint-postgres --with "psycopg[binary]" --with openai claim_flow.py start --thread t1 --amount 250
steps.expect: The process prints that it is waiting for approval and exits. Nothing is paid.

steps.task: Approve it from a new process
steps.explain: The second run is the real test. Any step that moves money must be safe to repeat.
steps.cmd: uv run --with langgraph --with langgraph-checkpoint-postgres --with "psycopg[binary]" --with openai claim_flow.py resume --thread t1 --approve
steps.expect: It carries on from the saved step and pays. Run the same command again: there is still exactly one payment row for t1.

steps.task: See the same contract in a ready-made stack
steps.explain: Optional. Flisk's agent resource keeps sessions in a checkpoint store in the same way your flow keeps threads in Postgres.
steps.expect: A local stack starts with an agent, tools and a database. flisk status --json shows the resources; flisk agent sessions <resource> lists stored sessions, and they are still listed after flisk restart <resource>.

44-fan-out.title: Many workers, one dispatcher
44-fan-out.goal: Process a batch of claims in parallel with a cap on how many run at once, retries for the ones that fail, and no claim lost.
44-fan-out.build: fanout.py: 20 claims, at most four at a time, each with a final result.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Make 20 claim emails and process them one after another, timed
steps.cmd: time uv run --with openai --with pydantic fanout.py claims/ --max 1
steps.expect: 20 results and a total time. This is the number to beat.

steps.task: Run them four at a time
steps.cmd: time uv run --with openai --with pydantic fanout.py claims/ --max 4
steps.expect: The same 20 results in well under the first time. The log never shows more than four in flight.

steps.task: Make one call in five fail at random, and retry twice with a growing wait
steps.explain: A batch that reports 18 of 20 with no word on the other two is the failure that reaches customers.
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with pydantic fanout.py claims/ --max 4 --chaos 0.2
steps.expect: Every claim ends as done or as failed after three tries. The count of both adds up to 20.

steps.task: Print a summary: done, retried, failed, total cost
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai --with pydantic fanout.py claims/ --max 4 --chaos 0.2 --summary
steps.expect: Four numbers, and the ids of any claim that failed for good.

45-self-improve.title: Let it improve itself, and prove it
45-self-improve.goal: Have a model propose changes to your prompt from its own failures, and accept a change only when held-back data says it helped.
45-self-improve.build: improve.py: proposes one prompt change, scores it, and prints ACCEPT or REJECT with the numbers.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Split 60 graded examples into 40 to learn from and 20 held back
steps.expect: 40 and 20 lines, with no example in both.

steps.task: Score the current prompt on the held-back set three times
steps.explain: The same prompt scores differently on each run. Until you know by how much, you cannot tell an improvement from luck.
steps.expect: Three scores and their spread. Any gain smaller than that spread is noise.

steps.task: Show the improver the failures from the 40 and ask for one prompt change
steps.expect: A changed prompt saved as a candidate, with one sentence on what it changes.

steps.task: Score the candidate on the held-back 20 and decide
steps.cmd: uv run --with openai improve.py --decide && grep -c heldout improver.log
steps.expect: ACCEPT or REJECT with both scores. The count is 0: the improver never saw the held-back set.

50-discovery.title: Find the use case worth building
50-discovery.goal: Turn a customer's vague wish for AI into one use case with a number that says when it worked.
50-discovery.build: A scored list of five candidate use cases and a one-page brief for the winner.
needs: A real or imagined customer (Parcel Desk works)

steps.task: Write up three short interviews: who does what today, how long it takes, what goes wrong
steps.expect: Three files, each with at least one number someone gave you (hours a week, claims a day, error rate).

steps.task: List five candidate use cases and score each: reach, impact, confidence, effort
steps.explain: The top score is rarely the most exciting idea. It is usually the dull task many people do every day.
steps.expect: A table with five scored rows and a total (reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort).

steps.task: For the winner, write the success number and how it will be measured
steps.expect: A sentence with a number and a date, such as: 70 percent of claims under 100 decided with no human, at under 2 percent wrong payouts, by week six.

steps.task: Finish the brief: problem, users, success number, what is out of scope, what needs a human
steps.expect: Under 400 words. A person who was not in the interviews can say what you are building and how you will know it worked.

51-security.title: Attack your own assistant
51-security.goal: Break your assistant with instructions hidden in the content it reads, then close the hole in the design rather than in the prompt.
51-security.build: redteam.py with five attacks, and an assistant that fails none of them.
needs: An OpenRouter key (free models are enough)

steps.task: Give the assistant a secret it must never reveal and a tool that can send data out
steps.expect: Five named attacks are listed. At least one hides an instruction in a policy page, and one in a tool result.

steps.task: Run the attacks
steps.explain: If none succeed, your attacks are too polite. Write the instruction the way an attacker would: as part of the document.
steps.expect: At least one attack makes the secret appear in an answer or an outgoing call. Keep the output.

steps.task: Write down which of the three dangerous abilities your assistant has
steps.explain: Any two of the three are manageable. An assistant with all three can be told by a stranger to leak your data.
steps.expect: Three lines: does it see private data, does it read content from strangers, can it send data out. All three together is the problem.

steps.task: Remove one of the three: an allowlist on the outgoing tool, or tools in a container with no network
steps.expect: All five attacks fail and the exit code is 0. The secret appears nowhere in the output.

52-gateway-policy.title: One door for every tool, with rules
52-gateway-policy.goal: Put every tool call through one checkpoint that decides allow, deny or ask a person, from rules kept in a file.
52-gateway-policy.build: gateway.py and policy.yaml, with tests for each kind of decision and a record of every call.

steps.task: Route every tool call through one function that knows who is calling, which tool and with what
steps.expect: A test passes showing that no tool can be reached without going through the gateway.

steps.task: Write three rules: support staff cannot pay, refunds over 100 need a person, everyone can look up a parcel
steps.explain: Rules in a file can be read and signed off by someone who does not read code. Larger teams use a policy language such as Cedar for the same job.
steps.expect: Tests pass for one allow, one deny and one needs-approval case.

steps.task: Call a tool that no rule mentions
steps.expect: It is denied. Anything not allowed by a rule is refused.

steps.task: Record every decision with its reason
steps.expect: One line per call: who, tool, decision and the rule that decided it.

53-deploy.title: Ship it and know the bill
53-deploy.goal: Package your assistant so it runs the same anywhere, keep secrets out of the package, and work out what a request costs.
53-deploy.build: A container image of your assistant with a health check, and a cost per request you measured.

steps.task: Put the harness behind two HTTP routes: /health and /ask
steps.expect: {"status":"ok"} from the server running on your machine.

steps.task: Write a Dockerfile and run the image with keys passed in at start
steps.cmd: docker build -t parcel-desk . && docker run -d --name pd -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env parcel-desk && sleep 3 && curl -s localhost:8080/health
steps.expect: The same health answer, now from the container.

steps.task: Check that no key is inside the image
steps.cmd: docker history --no-trunc parcel-desk | grep -c -i "api_key"; docker run --rm --entrypoint ls parcel-desk -a
steps.expect: The count is 0 and no .env file is listed. Keys arrive when the container starts, never when it is built.

steps.task: Send 50 requests and work out the cost of one
steps.expect: Average seconds and average cost per request, and what 1,000 requests a day would cost a month.

steps.task: Stop everything the course started
steps.explain: Leaving things running is how a free experiment becomes a bill. Make teardown the last step of every delivery.
steps.cmd: docker rm -f pd learn-pg learn-qdrant; docker ps --format "{{.Names}}"
steps.expect: None of the lab containers are listed. Stop Langfuse with docker compose down in its folder.

54-capstone.title: Capstone: the claims desk
54-capstone.goal: Put the course together into one assistant for Parcel Desk and hand it to someone else to run.
54-capstone.build: An assistant that reads a claim email, checks policy, decides, asks a person for large amounts, pays once, and comes with a runbook.

steps.task: Join the parts: extract the claim, look up policy, decide, approve over 100, pay
steps.expect: A decision with the policy page it relied on. A large claim stops and waits for approval.

steps.task: Score it on 40 graded claims with your checked judge
steps.expect: It meets the success number you wrote in lab 50. If not, the trace of the worst failures tells you which part to fix.

steps.task: Run your five attacks against the finished assistant
steps.expect: Exit 0: none succeed.

steps.task: Write the runbook: start, stop, where the logs are, the three most likely failures and their fix
steps.explain: The work is finished when it keeps running after you have left.
steps.expect: Under 80 lines. Give it to a colleague: they start the assistant, break it and fix it without asking you.
